hints: Place queens one row at a time.
A candidate conflicts if its column or either diagonal is occupied.
Track columns and both diagonal directions.
Count one solution after all rows are filled.
title: N-Queens II Problem

notes: Place one queen in each row and reject positions sharing a column or diagonal.
For n <= 9, backtracking with pruning is sufficient.
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [arg1, arg2, ...]

sampleTestCases.explanation: There are two distinct solutions to the 4-queens puzzle as shown.
For this input, applying the required rules of N-Queens II produces 1.

content.problemStatement:
Task: The **n-queens** puzzle is the problem of placing `n` queens on an `n x n` chessboard such that no two queens attack each other.

You receive an integer `n`, output *the number of distinct solutions to the **n-queens puzzle***.

notes: Expected output is the JSON-serialised integer count returned by totalNQueens.
Conflict checks are constant time with column and diagonal occupancy arrays.
solution.approach: Use row-by-row backtracking while tracking occupied columns and the two diagonal directions. Count a solution when all n rows are filled.

better.complexity: O(n!) worst-case time and O(n) auxiliary space.
better.description: Backtrack one row at a time and prune conflicting columns and diagonals immediately.

optimal.complexity: O(n!) worst-case time and O(n) auxiliary space.
optimal.description: Use pruned row-by-row backtracking with compact occupancy state; bitmasks can make conflict checks faster.

bruteForce.complexity: O(n! * n) time and O(n) extra space.
bruteForce.description: Enumerate row placements and test completed boards for conflicts.

code.C++: class Solution{int n;bool c[9],a[17],b[17];int dfs(int r){if(r==n)return 1;int ans=0;for(int j=0;j<n;j++){int x=r-j+n-1,y=r+j;if(c[j]||a[x]||b[y])continue;c[j]=a[x]=b[y]=true;ans+=dfs(r+1);c[j]=a[x]=b[y]=false;}return ans;}public:int totalNQueens(int n){this->n=n;memset(c,0,sizeof(c));memset(a,0,sizeof(a));memset(b,0,sizeof(b));return dfs(0);}};
code.Java: class Solution{public int totalNQueens(int n){boolean[] c=new boolean[n],a=new boolean[2*n-1],b=new boolean[2*n-1];return dfs(0,n,c,a,b);}private int dfs(int r,int n,boolean[] c,boolean[] a,boolean[] b){if(r==n)return 1;int ans=0;for(int j=0;j<n;j++){int x=r-j+n-1,y=r+j;if(c[j]||a[x]||b[y])continue;c[j]=a[x]=b[y]=true;ans+=dfs(r+1,n,c,a,b);c[j]=a[x]=b[y]=false;}return ans;}}

followUps: How can bitmasks speed up conflict checks?
How would the solution change if the actual boards had to be returned?
How can symmetry reduce the search for larger n?
learningObjectives: Represent search state with arrays or bitmasks.
